PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Zoo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how to visit the zoo like a real explorer — a plan, a quest, and kind quiet voices.

What is this?

A zoo is a big park where animals from all over the world live, and visitors walk from habitat to habitat to meet them: lions, penguins, giraffes and more.

What does it mean?

Meeting the world is the idea: the zoo is the only afternoon walk that passes through five continents.

What does the child need to know?

You need comfortable shoes, a map (or a plan of three animals), quiet voices, and walking feet — animals spook at shouting and running.

Why this matters

Most animals live where we cannot go — deserts, ice, treetops — the zoo brings them close enough to watch, learn about, and care about for the rest of your life.

What it teaches

Animal naming and grouping (big, small, striped, spotted), reading name plates (where it lives, what it eats), quiet-voice practice, and empathy for creatures with very different days than ours.

Words to learn

zooanimalhabitatlionpenguingiraffeelephantname platequestzookeeper

Say this to your child

“"The zoo! Here is the map — today we find THREE animals: the lion, the penguin, and the funny-named one! Quiet feet... look — the lion is stretching! The plate says: Africa, meat-eater, sleeps 20 hours. Wow. Penguins next!"”

Step by step

  1. Come in the gate and grab the map — every good expedition starts with a map.
  2. Pick the quest: three animals — one big, one small, one with a funny name. Write them down or remember them hard.
  3. Walk to animal one. Watch for a full minute — animals are busy; give them a moment to do something amazing.
  4. Read the name plate together: where does it live? what does it eat? Every plate is a tiny passport.
  5. Quiet voices all day, especially at the penguins — they are doing their important fish business. Three animals, deeply seen, beats thirty rushed ones.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the gates stand open under the big ZOO sign with round bushes standing guard — the doors to the one walk in town that crosses five continents.

Ask your child

"What do the name plates tell us?" (the animal’s name, where it lives, what it eats) "What kind of voices at the zoo?" (quiet ones) "How many animals on the quest?" (three — one big, one small, one funny-named)

What your child can say or do

Your child might adopt the penguin enclosure as a second home, narrate the lion like a nature documentary, or remember the okapi’s funny name for a full year and deploy it at dinner parties.

Out in the real world

The zoo is the same word on both shores, but the penguin feeding is the universal favorite in the US, UK and Canada. The gates on the card open onto the first geography lesson a child ever takes — every animal brings its own map.

Try it together

Pick three animals before you go — one big, one small, one with a funny name — and make them the quest. Read each plate out loud: three real facts beat a rushed lap of everything.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we read at every enclosure?" (the name plate — where it lives, what it eats) "How do we walk at the zoo?" (quiet feet, walking, no running)

This lesson pairs with the Zoo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
